fields.h1: Build Calendar Automation Around Your Team's Real Availability
fields.hero_description: Build calendar automation that books meetings only where everyone is free and saves each one to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: Inside the Calendar App Emergent Builds
fields.features_subheading: Booking rules tend to live in one coordinator's head. The app Emergent builds runs them against your team's calendars.
fields.feature_1:
Free and busy times read before any offer

The app asks Google Calendar or Outlook which hours are taken before it offers a slot. A candidate or customer picks from open times only, and nobody checks four calendars by hand.
fields.feature_2:
Booking rules described in plain English

Tell Emergent your rules the way you would brief an assistant: no calls before 10 AM, 15 minutes between external meetings, Fridays kept for internal work. Emergent builds the logic.
fields.feature_3:
A reminder first, then a named person

Pick when a reminder goes out by email, and how close to the start an unconfirmed booking can get before a named person on your team hears about it in Slack or in the app.
fields.feature_4:
Each booking stored as a row you own

Every meeting the app books or cancels is saved, with its owner and the form or CRM record behind it, to a database you own. Next quarter's routing rules start from that history.
fields.feature_5:
Meeting hours on a live dashboard

The dashboard adds up each person's hours in meetings as events land on their calendars. A manager sees who is close to the weekly limit by Tuesday, while meetings can still move.
fields.feature_6:
Your scheduling code in your GitHub

Export the full code of the app to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Anyone on your team can read each booking rule, change how ties break, and run it next to your other code.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Calendar Jobs Worth Handing to an App
fields.tab_content_1:
Odile picks Thursday from 3 open slots

Brackenfold Analytics needs a 90-minute panel for candidate Odile Pelletier with Dario Kesterton, Hannelore Brisk, and Lionel Ostberg. The app reads their calendars and offers Odile 3 slots when all of them are free. She picks Thursday at 10:00 AM, and the panel lands on four calendars, hers included.
fields.tab_content_2:
With 4 demos booked, Saoirse gets the next one

Corrigan Freight asks Tilwick Software for a demo. Your rule gives each demo to the rep with the fewest demos booked this week: Saoirse Malin has 4, Bram Telford 6, and Lionel Ishikawa 7. The 30-minute demo goes on Saoirse's calendar for Tuesday at 2:00 PM, with a direct message to her.
fields.tab_content_3:
No reply 4 hours out means a call from the desk

Fernmoor Auto Care emails every customer a reminder 24 hours before a service appointment. Nadia Ferreira's brake inspection is Friday at 1:00 PM, and she has not confirmed by 9:00 AM, 4 hours before it starts. Service desk lead Tobias Quennell gets a direct message to call her.
fields.tab_content_4:
26 hours of meetings for Garrett, limit 20

Sparrowgate Architects caps meetings at a 20-hour limit per person each week. One of the four people on the studio team is past it: Garrett Wexley, at 26 hours. His bar turns red, and a card shows the 6 hours he would need to move to get back under the cap.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to turn your team's booking rules into calendar automation that reads real availability, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the hardest meeting to book
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write each booking rule as a sentence
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Name an owner for each exception
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Describe the app in a prompt
fields.howto_step_1_des: Count the emails it took to book your last 10 interviews, demos, or service appointments. Start with the meeting type that needed the most messages per booking. Its rules become the first version of the app, and the other meeting types follow once that one runs cleanly.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write the rules as you would explain them to a new coordinator: who joins, how long it runs, the earliest start time, and the gap between meetings. Keep the numbers exact, such as 90 minutes for a panel or 15 minutes between external calls.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Decide who gets told when a booking goes wrong: an unconfirmed appointment, a canceled demo, or a candidate who never picks a slot. Name one person for each case instead of a shared inbox, and choose Slack or email for each one.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Open Emergent and describe the app in plain English, with the meeting names your team already uses. Include the rules from step 2 and the people from step 3. Emergent builds the booking page, the routing logic, and the dashboard from that prompt.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Connect the calendars the app reads
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect Google Calendar or Outlook through their APIs, along with the CRM or form that starts each booking. Grant the access the app needs to see availability and add events, then test it on one person's calendar before adding the whole team.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Book real meetings through the app
fields.howto_step_6_des: Run a handful of real bookings through the app before it goes live, including one with a conflict and one that gets canceled. Check each event on every attendee's calendar, then find the matching row in the database for each booking.
fields.howto_step_7_des: When a rule needs to change, such as a new 20-hour weekly cap on meetings, describe the change in a new prompt. Emergent changes the app, and the dashboard shows how the next week's calendars look under the new rule.

faq_plan.a: Calendar automation is software that books and tracks meetings by rules instead of by email back-and-forth. It reads who is free, picks a time that fits the rules, writes the event to each attendee's calendar, and sends the follow-ups. The Google Calendar API, for one, returns free/busy information for a set of calendars, which is the data every booking rule starts from.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up calendar automation?
faq_plan.a: Pick one meeting type, write its booking rules as sentences, and describe them in a prompt to Emergent's AI automation builder. Emergent builds the app and its database, and the app connects to the calendar your team already uses through its API. Run five real bookings through it before the whole team switches over.

faq_plan.q: What does meeting scheduling automation do after a time is booked?
faq_plan.a: It runs the follow-ups: the confirmation, the reminders, a reschedule link, and the update when someone cancels. Give each one its own timing as a rule. Reminders the app writes onto a Google Calendar event have a ceiling, since the maximum number of override reminders is 5.

faq_plan.q: What permissions does calendar automation need?
faq_plan.a: It needs access to availability, plus access to events if it books meetings. Google Calendar's calendar.events scope is the wider grant, letting an app view and edit events on all your calendars. Request it only for apps that write events. Granting and revoking that access across staff accounts is a job for it automation.

faq_plan.q: How does calendar automation avoid double bookings?
faq_plan.a: It checks availability twice: once when it offers slots, and again the moment someone picks one. A slot offered at 9:00 can be taken by 9:05. The second check decides whether the event is written or the person sees fresh times. With Emergent, every booking the app makes lands in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: Should calendar automation add buffer time between meetings?
faq_plan.a: Yes, for meetings with people outside your team. Set a fixed gap, such as 15 minutes after each external call, and the app counts that time as busy when it offers slots. Leave internal stand-ups without a buffer, or the day fills with short gaps nobody can book.

faq_plan.q: Can calendar automation create follow-up tasks after a meeting?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The app can watch for an event to end and create a task for its owner, such as sending a proposal within 2 days of a demo. Work that never touches a calendar, like a weekly report reminder, fits better in task automation. Emergent sets no task cap, and a week of back-to-back demos runs like a quiet one.

faq_plan.q: How does calendar automation handle time zones?
faq_plan.a: It stores each time with its time zone and converts only when it shows the time to a person. Google Calendar events name the zone in a format the API describes as an IANA Time Zone Database name. Show each invitee slots in their own zone, and keep the booking rules, such as no calls before 10 AM, in the host's zone.

faq_plan.q: What should calendar automation do when a meeting is canceled?
faq_plan.a: It should free the slot and tell everyone on the invite. For a canceled demo, the app removes the event from the rep's calendar, updates the CRM deal, and offers the requester new times. Keep canceled bookings in the history: the dashboard can then show how often each meeting type falls through.

faq_plan.q: Can customers reschedule through calendar automation without calling?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Put a reschedule link in the confirmation email that shows only open times, and the app moves the event on every attendee's calendar. Requests that arrive by chat or email instead of the link belong to customer service automation, which can answer the message and pass the new time to the booking app.

plan.angle: The query mixes how-to posts about one calendar app with roundups of scheduling tools that each solve one job. This page shows calendar automation as one app that sits on the calendars a team already uses: a 90-minute interview panel booked only where three interviewers are free, demo requests routed to the rep with the fewest demos this week, service appointments confirmed or flagged to the desk 4 hours out, and a dashboard that shows who is past 20 hours of meetings. It stays off generic task lists, help-desk tickets and Slack-only alerts, which sibling pages own.
